newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-GTE seen as an emerging powerhouse.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-GTE seen as an emerging powerhouse.

text.p: GTE Corp's $616 million deal to buy BBN Corp and its two major networking alliances will help transform it from a regionalized local telephone company into a powerhouse providing nationwide long-distance services and Internet access, analysts said.
Chief executive Charles Lee told reporters on Tuesday that GTE's goal was to become a $34-$38 billion "market-leading telecommunications" company by 2001.
"We really think of it as a change in the overall direction of the company," said Bear Stearns' Bill Deatherage.

"They are going from concentrating on their local franchise areas into addressing a nationwide market," Deatherage said. "They are also adding capacities to approach a full spectrum of business customers with data, Internet and long-distance services."
In the short-term, GTE said its earnings will suffer as it invests in developing a high-speed national network.

As part of that effort, GTE also announced an alliance with Cisco Systems Inc to develop an end-to-end, next-generation network. GTE's purchases of Cisco products could exceed $1 billion during the next five years.
GTE said its 1997 earnings growth for 1997 would be flat to slightly positive, with moderate growth in 1998. In 1999, GTE expects earnings growth of about 13 to 15 percent.
"We are making an investment," Lee told reporters. "In three and a half years, we will be back to the same level (of earnings) and we will grow earnings at around 15 percent."

GTE's second investment involves an agreement providing it with the right to use a dark fiber optic network under construction by Qwest Communications Corp, which is privately held. GTE would not disclose how much it was spending under the Qwest deal.
An industry source estimated GTE would spend about $485 million on the Qwest deal.

GTE is acquiring the rights to use 24 dark fibers, installed along a 13,000-mile coast-to-coast network that Qwest is currently building. Qwest plans to retain about 48 fibers for its own network use. Dark fibers are those without any networking equipment installed on them.
"It is like buying a railroad track, and they are buying their own locomotive and cars," said a Qwest spokesman.
Qwest will run its own long-distance services parallel to GTE's. The network is scheduled for completion in late 1998.

Qwest's network -- combined with BBN's Internet backbone and bulk dial-up Internet access, Web hosting, security and consulting services -- will give GTE the tools to become a leading telecommunications player, analysts said..

GTE now offers local and wireless services in 29 states and long distance in all 50 states. It has provided Internet access for about a year, using UUNET Technologies Inc's Internet backbone. UUNET is a unit of WorldCom Inc.
"They have many geographically dispersed properties, so going national makes sense," said Robert Wilkes, a Brown Brothers Harriman analyst.
"They are targeting a market opportunity. Data (services) is growing a lot faster than voice," Wilkes said.

In the past few weeks, speculation emerged that AT&T Corp was looking at buying BBN, which is one of the pioneering developers of the Internet, having created the ARPAnet 28 years ago. The ARPAnet -- an experimental network, where theories and software were tested -- was the forerunner to the current Internet.
GTE, BBN and AT&T all declined to comment on whether BBN held discussions with other parties. But analysts said a sale of BBN to AT&T would not have made sense.
"I don't think AT&T has any interest in them," said Frank Dzubeck, president of Communications Network Architects, in Washington. "(AT&T) has some strategic, tactical issues to deal with right now."

AT&T currently runs some of its Internet access services on BBN's Internet backbone, but a spokesman for AT&T WorldNet said that AT&T is gradually moving its Internet services onto its own network backbone. The two companies are also involved in a dispute over their current contract. The spokesman declined to provide details about the dispute, or how it might be affected by GTE's deal to buy BBN.
"We can't say what the effect of the acquisition will be on the duration of the contract," said an AT&T spokesman.
Analysts said that AT&T and other telecommunications providers seeking to enter the Internet access arena, were probably concerned about the aggressive moves by GTE.
"This is the type of competition that the Telcom Act (of 1996) has envisioned," said Deatherage. "The regulators would applaud these kind of deals."
